lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Hello everyone, good evening, and welcome to the class. I know many of you have come straight from the branch. So first, just relax for a minute. How was the day? Busy? It's always busy, right?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay. Notifications on silent, please. Keep a pen and a calculator nearby. Today we need the calculator only for one small thing, I promise.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Let me start with a question. How many of you have handled an export or import file at your branch? Just think about it. Some of you do it every day. Many of you have never touched one. Both are fine.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Because today's topic is Incoterms. And here's why it's worth your time. In the papers we checked, letters of credit came up in six out of the last seven exams. And Incoterms questions came up in three of them. One was a full case study.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And honestly, these are easy marks. It's only eleven rules, and one picture holds all of them. No heavy theory, I promise. Stay with me for fifteen minutes, and this topic is yours. Shall we start?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, picture this. A knitwear exporter from Tiruppur. She has a buyer in Rotterdam, in the Netherlands. The deal is for forty-eight thousand US dollars, and it's backed by a letter of credit opened by the buyer's bank.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: In the contract and in the LC, the price is written like this: C-I-F Rotterdam, Incoterms twenty twenty. Keep that line in mind. We'll come back to it again and again.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now, she packs the goods, sends them to Chennai port, and the container is loaded on the ship. She gets the bill of lading. Everything looks perfect.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Two days later, there's a storm at sea. And her container goes overboard. Lost. All forty-eight thousand dollars of knitwear, at the bottom of the sea.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Next morning she's at your branch, very worried. She says, the goods are gone. Will I still get my money? Whose loss is this, mine or the buyer's?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, let me ask you. Under C-I-F, whose loss is it? The seller's, or the buyer's? Think for a second. Lock your answer in.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay. I know what many of you are thinking. C-I-F means cost, insurance and freight. The seller paid the freight, the seller bought the insurance. So the sea journey is the seller's job. So it's the seller's loss.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And a few of you are thinking, hmm, wait. Maybe once the goods are on the ship, they're the buyer's problem.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Well, that second group is right. Under C-I-F, the risk moves to the buyer the moment the goods are on board the ship at the port of shipment. Here, Chennai. After that, the sea is the buyer's risk.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So why does the seller pay for freight and insurance at all? See, here's the thing. She's paying for a journey that's already at the buyer's risk. She arranges the ship and buys the insurance, but the insurance protects the buyer.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So what happens now? She hands her documents to the bank. The bill of lading, the invoice, the insurance policy. If they match the LC, the bank pays. Remember, banks deal with documents, not goods. That's UCP six hundred, article five.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the buyer? He gets the insurance policy along with the documents. So he claims from the insurer. Nobody is left holding the loss. That's the whole point.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: If you said "seller", don't feel bad. Almost everybody does the first time. The word "insurance" in the name makes it sound like the seller is carrying the risk. She isn't.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, what is an Incoterm? It's a set of rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce, the ICC. Three letters, a place, and the version. Like "C-I-F Rotterdam, Incoterms twenty twenty".

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And those three letters answer three questions for the buyer and seller. One. Where does the seller deliver, and so, where does the risk pass? Two. Who pays which costs? Three. Who does the customs work, export and import?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now be careful here, because the exam loves this. Incoterms do not decide the price. They don't decide how or when payment is made. And they don't decide when ownership of the goods passes. That's for the sales contract.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Also, Incoterms are not law. They apply only when the parties write them into the contract. That's why we always add the version, Incoterms twenty twenty. An old contract could still say twenty ten.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the version we follow today is Incoterms twenty twenty. It came into force on the first of January, twenty twenty. ICC has only just begun work on the next version, so for your exam, twenty twenty is the answer.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, that's part one. Still with me? Good. You already know the most important thing: risk and cost are two different things. Hold on to that.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now stretch for a second if you like. Part two is the picture that holds all eleven rules. I need full attention for this one.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, here's our picture. A road. On the left, the seller's door. On the right, the buyer's door. And seven stops in between. Let me walk you through them.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Stop one, the seller's own premises. Stop two, the goods are handed over to the carrier. Stop three, alongside the ship at the port. Stop four, on board the ship.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Then comes the sea, or the air, or the long road. Stop five, the goods arrive at the destination, ready to be unloaded. Stop six, unloaded. And stop seven, cleared through import customs, with the duty paid.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And two markers move on this road. The red baton is the risk. Wherever the baton is handed over, from there, any loss is the buyer's. The blue line is the cost. It shows how far the seller pays.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now let's put the eleven rules on the road, from the seller's door to the buyer's door. Just watch, don't write. The card at the end has all of it.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: First, E-X-W. Ex Works. The seller just keeps the goods ready at her own premises. The buyer comes, loads the truck, and does everything after that. Even the export clearance. This is the least the seller can do.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Next, F-C-A. Free Carrier. The seller hands the goods to the carrier the buyer has chosen. If that happens at the seller's own premises, the seller also loads them. And she clears them for export.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: F-A-S, Free Alongside Ship. The goods are placed next to the ship at the port of shipment. And F-O-B, Free on Board. The goods are loaded on board the ship. In all these F rules, the buyer pays the main freight.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now the C rules. These are the clever ones. C-F-R, cost and freight. And C-I-F, cost, insurance and freight. The risk passes on board the ship, same place as F-O-B. But the seller pays the freight all the way to the destination port.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Then C-P-T, Carriage Paid To. And C-I-P, Carriage and Insurance Paid To. Here the risk passes when the goods are handed to the first carrier. But again, the seller pays the carriage up to the destination.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So see what happens with the C rules. The baton is handed over at the start, but the blue line keeps running to the end. Two different points. That's exactly where our Tiruppur exporter's case sits.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And finally, the D rules. Delivered. D-A-P, Delivered at Place. The goods arrive at the destination, ready to be unloaded, and the buyer unloads them.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: D-P-U, Delivered at Place Unloaded. Same, but the seller also unloads them. It's the only rule where the seller unloads at the destination. And D-D-P, Delivered Duty Paid. The seller even clears import customs and pays the duty. This is the most the seller can do.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, E-X-W at one end, seller does the least. D-D-P at the other end, seller does the most. Everything else sits in between. That's a favourite question.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And customs is simple. Export clearance is the seller's job in every rule, except E-X-W. Import clearance is the buyer's job in every rule, except D-D-P.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Easy way to remember the four groups: E for exit, the goods leave from the seller's door. F for free, the seller is free of the main freight. C for carriage paid, but the risk has already gone. And D for delivered, right there at the destination.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, quick check. Everyone with me? Let's test it. Under C-P-T, where does the risk pass? Some of you are saying at the destination, because carriage is paid till there. Others are saying when the goods go to the carrier. What do you say?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: When it's handed to the first carrier. Did you get it? Good. Because it's a C rule. The seller pays the carriage, but the baton has already gone. Same story as C-I-F.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now, look at the road once more. Four of these rules use the ship itself as the point. F-A-S, alongside the ship. And F-O-B, C-F-R and C-I-F, on board. These four are only for sea and inland waterway transport. The other seven work for any mode, even air, rail or road, or more than one together.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And here's a trap the exam likes. Containers. A container is usually handed over at the container terminal, before it goes on board. So for container cargo, ICC says F-C-A and C-I-P fit better than F-O-B and C-I-F.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And how many rules in all? Eleven. Seven for any mode, four for sea. That exact question, "how many Incoterms", came up twice in one exam cycle. Don't let anyone tell you thirteen. Thirteen was the old two thousand set.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: One more thing that changed in twenty twenty. There used to be a rule called D-A-T, Delivered at Terminal. In twenty twenty it became D-P-U, because now the goods can be unloaded at any place, not only a terminal.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, deep breath. That was the heaviest part, and you're through it. Eleven rules, one road. Now let's come to the part that touches your desk at the branch: insurance and the LC.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, in which rules does the seller have to buy insurance? Only two. C-I-F and C-I-P. The "I" in the name is the clue. In every other rule, if anybody insures the goods, it's the buyer, for his own protection.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And here's the twenty twenty change everybody asks about. Under C-I-P, the seller must buy wide cover, the Institute Cargo Clauses A. That's the all-risks kind. Under C-I-F, the minimum is still Clauses C, the basic kind. Unless the parties agree something else.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Why the difference? ICC's thinking is this. C-I-F is used a lot for bulk commodities at sea, where basic cover is the custom. C-I-P is used more for manufactured goods. So C-I-P got the bigger umbrella.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And how much cover? At least one hundred and ten percent of the contract price. Not one hundred. One hundred and ten. And the cover must be in the currency of the contract.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: The LC side says the same thing. Under UCP six hundred, article twenty-eight, if the LC is silent on the amount, the cover must be at least one hundred and ten percent of the C-I-F or C-I-P value.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, calculators out. Our exporter's price. Her goods on board at Chennai cost forty-five thousand dollars. That's her F-O-B value. Sea freight to Rotterdam, two thousand four hundred. Insurance premium, six hundred.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Add them up. Forty-five thousand, plus two thousand four hundred, plus six hundred. Forty-eight thousand dollars. That's her C-I-F price. Cost, plus insurance, plus freight. The name is the formula.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now the minimum insurance cover. Forty-eight thousand, into one point one, equals. Fifty-two thousand eight hundred dollars. Simple. The same multiplier habit as before, no percent key needed.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Your turn. A C-I-P price of thirty thousand euros. What's the minimum cover? Pause the video and press the keys.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Done? Thirty thousand, into one point one. Thirty-three thousand euros. Did you get it? Great.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now be careful here, this is where people slip. Some of you will take one hundred and ten percent of the F-O-B value. That's wrong. The base is the C-I-F or C-I-P value. On our numbers, F-O-B would give you forty-nine thousand five hundred. Wrong option.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now think about what this means at the LC desk. If the LC says C-I-F or C-I-P, the seller's documents must include an insurance document. If it says F-O-B or F-C-A, the buyer insures, so the seller won't send one.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the insurance document must not be dated after the shipment date, unless it shows the cover started by then. Cover that starts after the goods have sailed is no cover at all. That's also article twenty-eight.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the bill of lading usually tells you who paid the freight. Under C and D rules you'd usually see "freight prepaid". Under F rules, "freight collect". It's a quick way to see whether the documents fit the term.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So let's go back to Tiruppur. Under C-I-F, the risk passed on board at Chennai. Her documents comply, so the LC pays her. The buyer claims on the insurance. Her lost container is the buyer's problem, and the buyer is covered.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, three quick questions before we finish. Answer each one before I do.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: One. Under which rule does the seller carry the most obligations?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: D-D-P. Delivered Duty Paid. Even import duty.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Two. Which rule replaced D-A-T in twenty twenty?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: D-P-U. Delivered at Place Unloaded.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Three. A C-I-F price of one lakh twenty-five thousand four hundred dollars. The LC says nothing about the insurance amount. What's the minimum cover?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: One lakh twenty-five thousand four hundred, into one point one. One lakh thirty-seven thousand nine hundred and forty dollars. Did you get all three? Very good.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So here's the whole lesson on one card. Step one: three letters decide three things. Where risk passes, who pays, who clears customs.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Step two: put the rule on the road. E at the seller's door, F at the carrier or the ship, D at the buyer's end.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Step three: for C rules, the baton and the blue line split. The risk goes early, the cost goes all the way.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And for insurance: only C-I-F and C-I-P, at least one hundred and ten percent. C-I-P with the bigger cover.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So next time an LC lands on your desk with three letters on it, you'll know exactly what they mean.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: That's it for today. Next class, we open the LC itself, and the UCP articles the exam keeps asking.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: One small homework. Draw the road once tonight, from memory, and put all eleven rules on it. Five minutes. Then do the practice questions. Okay, good night everyone, go and rest. See you in the next class.
